subject: Physics
stem: Two charged spherical conductors of radius \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are connected by a wire. Then the ratio of surface charge densities of the spheres \((\sigma_1/\sigma_2)\) is
solution:
When two conductors are connected by a conducting wire, then the two conductors should have same potential.
So, \(V_1 = V_2\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q_1}{R_1} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q_2}{R_2}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q_1}{R_1}\times\dfrac{R_1}{R_1} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q_2}{R_2}\times\dfrac{R_2}{R_2}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{Q_1 R_1}{4\pi R_1^2\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{Q_2 R_2}{4\pi R_2^2\varepsilon_0}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{\sigma_1 R_1}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{\sigma_2 R_2}{\varepsilon_0}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2} = \dfrac{R_2}{R_1}\)

subject: Physics
stem: The velocity of a small ball of mass \(M\) and density \(d\), when dropped in a container filled with glycerine becomes constant after some time. If the density of glycerine is \(\dfrac{d}{2}\), then the viscous force acting on the ball will be
solution:
Let \(F_v\) be the viscous force and \(F_B\) be the Buoyant force acting on the ball.
Then, when body moves with constant velocity
\(Mg = F_B + F_v\) \([a = 0]\)
\(F_v = Mg - F_B\)
\(= dVg - \dfrac{d}{2}\cdot Vg\) \((M = dVg)\), \(V\) = volume of ball.
\(= \dfrac{d}{2}Vg\)
\(F_v = \dfrac{M}{2}g\)

subject: Physics
subtopic: Force on Moving Charge Near Current-Carrying Wire
stem: An infinitely long straight conductor carries a current of 5 A as shown. An electron is moving with a speed of \(10^5\) m/s parallel to the conductor. The perpendicular distance between the electron and the conductor is 20 cm at an instant. Calculate the magnitude of the force experienced by the electron at that instant.
solution:
Magnetic field produced due to current carrying wire at point 'A'
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2I}{r}\)
\(B = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times2\times5}{20\times10^{-2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\times10^{-5}\) (Tesla), upward to the plane of paper
Now, force acting on electron due to this field
\(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\)
\(|\vec{F}| = 1.6\times10^{-19}\times10^5\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times10^{-5}\)
\(= 0.8\times10^{-19}\) N
\(|\vec{F}| = 8\times10^{-20}\) N

subject: Physics
stem: A dipole is placed in an electric field as shown. In which direction will it move? (The dipole has \(+q\) on the left and \(-q\) on the right, aligned along a non-uniform field \(\vec{E}\) that is stronger to the left and weaker to the right.)
options: Towards the left as its potential energy will increase.
Towards the right as its potential energy will decrease.
Towards the left as its potential energy will decrease.
Towards the right as its potential energy will increase.
solution:
Potential energy of electric dipole in external electric field \(U = -\vec{P}\cdot\vec{E}\)
Angle between electric field and electric dipole is 180°
\(U = -PE\cos\theta\)
\(U = -PE\cos180°\)
\(U = +PE\)
On moving towards right electric field strength decrease therefore potential energy decrease.
Net force on electric dipole is towards right and net torque acting on it is zero.
So, it will move towards right.

subject: Physics
stem: A lens of large focal length and large aperture is best suited as an objective of an astronomical telescope since
options: A large aperture contributes to the quality and visibility of the images.
A large area of the objective ensures better light gathering power.
A large aperture provides a better resolution.
solution:
With larger aperture of objective lens, the light gathering power in telescope is high.
Also, the resolving power or the ability to observe two objects distinctly also depends on the diameter of the objective. Thus objective of large diameter is preferred.
Also, with large diameters fainter objects can be observed. Hence it also contributes to the better quality and visibility of images.
Hence, all options are correct.

subject: Physics
stem:
A screw gauge gives the following readings when used to measure the diameter of a wire
Main scale reading : 0 mm
Circular scale reading : 52 divisions
Given that 1 mm on main scale corresponds to 100 divisions on the circular scale. The diameter of the wire from the above data is
solution:
Here, pitch of the screw gauge, \(P = 1\) mm
Number of circular division, \(n = 100\)
Thus least count \(LC = \dfrac{P}{n} = \dfrac{1}{100} = 0.01\) mm
\(= 0.001\) cm
So, diameter of the wire \(= MSR + (CSR\times LC)\)
\(= 0 + (52\times0.001\text{ cm})\)
\(= 0.052\) cm

subject: Physics
stem: A nucleus with mass number 240 breaks into two fragments each of mass number 120, the binding energy per nucleon of unfragmented nuclei is 7.6 MeV while that of fragments is 8.5 MeV. The total gain in the Binding Energy in the process is
solution:
Mass number of reactant = 240
\(BE\) per nucleon = 7.6 MeV
Mass number of products = 120
\(BE\) per nucleon of product = 8.5 MeV
Total gain in \(BE\) = \((BE)\) of products \(-\) \((BE)\) of reactants.
\(= [120 + 120]\times8.5 - [240]\times7.6\)
\(= (240)\times8.5 - 240\times7.6\)
\(= (2040 - 1824)\) MeV
Gain in \(BE\) = 216 MeV

subject: Physics
stem: A small block slides down on a smooth inclined plane, starting from rest at time \(t = 0\). Let \(S_n\) be the distance travelled by the block in the interval \(t = n - 1\) to \(t = n\). Then, the ratio \(\dfrac{S_n}{S_{n+1}}\) is
solution:
Suppose \(\theta\) is inclination of inclined plane acceleration along inclined plane \(a = g\sin\theta\)
\(S_n\) = distance travelled by object during \(n^{th}\) second.
Initial speed \(u = 0\)
By equation of uniformly accelerated motion
\(S_n = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)\)
\(S_n = 0 + \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{2}(2n-1) = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{2}(2n-1)\) ...(i)
Distance travelled during \((n+1)^{th}\) second.
\(S_{n+1} = 0 + \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{2}[2(n+1)-1] = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{2}(2n+1)\) ...(ii)
Dividing equations (i) and (ii)
\(\dfrac{S_n}{S_{n+1}} = \dfrac{(2n-1)}{(2n+1)}\)

subject: Physics
stem: Find the value of the angle of emergence from the prism. Refractive index of the glass is \(\sqrt{3}\). (The prism is a right-angled prism with a 60° angle; the ray strikes normally on the hypotenuse face.)
solution:
From the ray diagram shown in the figure.
At point \(P\), from Snell's law
\(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\mu_{air}}{\mu_{Prism}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{\sin30°}{\sin e} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) \((\angle r = \angle e\) emergent angle)
\(\Rightarrow \sin e = \sqrt{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(\Rightarrow \angle e = 60°\)

subject: Physics
stem: A spring is stretched by 5 cm by a force 10 N. The time period of the oscillations when a mass of 2 kg is suspended by it is
solution:
For a spring, \(kx = F\)
given \(x = 5\) cm, \(F = 10\) N
\(\Rightarrow k(5\times10^{-2}) = 10\)
\(\Rightarrow k = \dfrac{1000}{5} = 200\) N/m
Now, for spring-mass system undergoing SHM
\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\)
given, \(m = 2\) kg
\(\Rightarrow T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{200}} = \dfrac{2\pi}{10} = 0.628\) s

subject: Physics
stem: A convex lens 'A' of focal length 20 cm and a concave lens 'B' of focal length 5 cm are kept along the same axis with a distance 'd' between them. If a parallel beam of light falling on 'A' leaves 'B' as a parallel beam, then the distance 'd' in cm will be
solution:
Parallel beam of light after refraction from convex lens converge at the focus of convex lens. In question it is given light after refraction pass through concave lens becomes parallel. Therefore light refracted from convex lens virtually meet at focus of concave lens.
According to above ray diagram \(d = f_A - f_B\)
\(= 20 - 5 = 15\) cm

stem:
Column-I gives certain physical terms associated with flow of current through a metallic conductor.
Column-II gives some mathematical relations involving electrical quantities. Match Column-I and Column-II with appropriate relations.

| Column-I | Column-II |
|---|---|
| (A) Drift Velocity | (P) \(\dfrac{m}{ne^2\rho}\) |
| (B) Electrical Resistivity | (Q) \(nev_d\) |
| (C) Relaxation Period | (R) \(\dfrac{eE}{m}\tau\) |
| (D) Current Density | (S) \(\dfrac{E}{J}\) |
solution:
Drift velocity, \(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\)
Electrical resistivity, \(\rho = \dfrac{1}{\sigma} = \dfrac{E}{J}\)
Relaxation period, \(\tau = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\rho}\)
Current density, \(J = \dfrac{I}{A} = nev_d\)
(A) - (R), (B) - (S), (C) - (P), (D) - (Q)

subject: Physics
stem: The electron concentration in an \(n\)-type semiconductor is the same as hole concentration in a \(p\)-type semiconductor. An external field (electric) is applied across each of them. Compare the currents in them.
options: No current will flow in \(p\)-type, current will only flow in \(n\)-type
solution:
The current through a semiconductor is
\(I = neAv_d\)
\(I = neA\mu E\)
\(\dfrac{I_n}{I_p} = \dfrac{n_e eA\mu_e E}{n_h eA\mu_h E}\)
\(\dfrac{I_n}{I_p} = \dfrac{\mu_e}{\mu_h}\)
\(\because \mu_e > \mu_h\)
\(\Rightarrow I_n > I_p\)

subject: Physics
stem: A radioactive nucleus \({}_{Z}^{A}X\) undergoes spontaneous decay in the sequence \({}_{Z}^{A}X \rightarrow {}_{Z-1}B \rightarrow {}_{Z-3}C \rightarrow {}_{Z-2}D\), where \(Z\) is the atomic number of element \(X\). The possible decay particles in the sequence are
solution:
On \(\beta^+\) decay atomic number decreases by 1
On \(\beta^{-1}\) decay atomic number increases by 1
On \(\alpha\) decay atomic number decreases by 2
\({}_{Z}^{A}X \xrightarrow{\beta^+ \text{ decay}} {}_{Z-1}B \xrightarrow{\alpha \text{ decay}} {}_{Z-3}C \xrightarrow{\beta^- \text{ decay}} {}_{Z-2}D\)
Hence correct order of decay are \(\beta^+, \alpha, \beta^-\)

subject: Physics
stem: Water falls from a height of 60 m at the rate of 15 kg/s to operate a turbine. The losses due to frictional force are 10% of the input energy. How much power is generated by the turbine? \((g = 10\text{ m/s}^2)\)
solution:
Incident power on turbine = \(\dfrac{d(mgh)}{dt}\)
\(= gh\dfrac{dm}{dt}\)
\(= 10\times60\times15\)
\(= 9000\) W
Now, losses are 10%
\(\therefore\) power generated = \(\left(1 - \dfrac{10}{100}\right)\times9000\)
\(= 8100\) W
\(= 8.1\) kW

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The number of photons per second on an average emitted by the source of monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm, when it delivers the power of \(3.3\times10^{-3}\) watt will be \((h = 6.6\times10^{-34}\) J s)
solution:
The power of a source is given as
\(P = \dfrac{E}{t} = \dfrac{n}{t}\left(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\right)\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{n}{t} = \dfrac{P}{\left(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\right)}\)
(Here \(\dfrac{n}{t}\) is number of photons emitted per second)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{n}{t} = \dfrac{3.3\times10^{-3}\times6\times10^{-7}}{6.6\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}\)
\(= 10^{16}\) photons per second

subject: Physics
subtopic: Direction of E and B Fields
stem: For a plane electromagnetic wave propagating in \(x\)-direction, which one of the following combination gives the correct possible directions for electric field \((E)\) and magnetic field \((B)\) respectively?
solution:
Direction of propagation of electromagnetic waves is along \(\vec{E}\times\vec{B}\)
Given that direction of propagation is along \(x\)-axis
(1) \((\hat{j}+\hat{k})\times(\hat{j}+\hat{k}) = 0\)
(2) \((-\hat{j}+\hat{k})\times(-\hat{j}-\hat{k}) = 2\hat{i}\)
(3) \((\hat{j}+\hat{k})\times[-(\hat{j}+\hat{k})] = 0\)
(4) \((-\hat{j}+\hat{k})\times(-\hat{j}+\hat{k}) = 0\)
\(\therefore\) Option (2) is correct.

subject: Physics
stem: The effective resistance of a parallel connection that consists of four wires of equal length, equal area of cross-section and same material is 0.25 \(\Omega\). What will be the effective resistance if they are connected in series?
solution:
All the wires are identical and of same material so they will have same value of resistance. Let it be \(R\). When these are (four) connected in parallel.
\(R_P = \dfrac{R}{4}\) \(\left(\dfrac{1}{R_P} = \dfrac{1}{R_1}+\dfrac{1}{R_2}+\dfrac{1}{R_3}+\dfrac{1}{R_4}\right)\)
Given \(R_P = 0.25\ \Omega\)
\(\therefore 0.25 = \dfrac{R}{4}\)
\(\therefore R = 1\ \Omega\)
Now these four resistances are arranged in series
\(R_S = R + R + R + R = 4R\)
\(\therefore R_S = 4\times1 = 4\ \Omega\)

subject: Physics
stem: In a potentiometer circuit a cell of EMF 1.5 V gives balance point at 36 cm length of wire. If another cell of EMF 2.5 V replaces the first cell, then at what length of the wire, the balance point occurs?
solution:
From the application of potentiometer to compare two cells of emfs \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) by balancing lengths \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\)
\(\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\)
\(\Rightarrow \ell_2 = \ell_1\left(\dfrac{E_2}{E_1}\right) = (36\text{ cm})\left(\dfrac{2.5\text{ V}}{1.5\text{ V}}\right)\)
\(= 60\) cm

subject: Physics
stem: Polar molecules are the molecules
options: Acquire a dipole moment only in the presence of electric field due to displacement of charges
Acquire a dipole moment only when magnetic field is absent
Having a permanent electric dipole moment
solution:
In polar molecules, the centre of positive charges does not coincide with the centre of negative charges.
Hence, these molecules have a permanent electric dipole moment of their own.

subject: Physics
stem: A parallel plate capacitor has a uniform electric field \(\vec{E}\) in the space between the plates. If the distance between the plates is \(d\) and the area of each plate is \(A\), the energy stored in the capacitor is \((\varepsilon_0 = \text{permittivity of free space})\)
solution:
Energy density associated with electric field is given by
\(u = \dfrac{dU}{dV} = \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\)
\(\Rightarrow dU = \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 dV\)
Total energy stored in the space between the capacitor will be
\(U = \int dU = \int\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 dV\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\int dV\) \([E\) is constant]
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 V = \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 Ad\) \([V = Ad]\)

stem: The equivalent capacitance of the combination shown in the figure is. (Two capacitors \(C\) in series form the outer branch, and a capacitor \(C\) bridges between their junction and the same two nodes, so its two plates are at the same potential.)
solution:

So the capacitor is short circuited. It does not store any charge.
The circuit can be redrawn as two capacitors \(C\) in parallel between \(A\) and \(B\).

Consider the following statements (A) and (B) and identify the correct answer.
(A) A zener diode is connected in reverse bias, when used as a voltage regulator.
(B) The potential barrier of \(p\)-\(n\) junction lies between 0.1 V to 0.3 V.
solution:
In reverse biased, after breakdown, voltage across the zener diode becomes constant. Therefore zener diode is connected in reverse biased when used as voltage regulator.
Potential barrier of silicon diode is nearly 0.7 V statement A is correct and statement B is incorrect.

subject: Physics
stem: A particle is released from height \(S\) from the surface of the Earth. At a certain height its kinetic energy is three times its potential energy. The height from the surface of earth and the speed of the particle at that instant are respectively
solution:
Let required height of body is \(y\).
When body from rest falls through height \((S - y)\) then under constant acceleration
\(v^2 = 0^2 + 2g(S - y)\)
\(v = \sqrt{2g(S - y)}\) ...(1)
When body is at height \(y\) above ground. Potential energy of body of mass \(m\)
\(U = mgy\)
As per given condition kinetic energy, \(K = 3U\)
\(\dfrac{1}{2}m(v)^2 = 3\times mg(y)\)
\(\dfrac{1}{2}\times m\times2g(S - y) = 3\times mgy\) (using (1))
\(S - y = 3y\)
\(\therefore y = \dfrac{S}{4}\) ...(2)
\(\therefore v = \sqrt{2\times g\left(S - \dfrac{S}{4}\right)} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3gS}{2}}\) ...(3)

subject: Physics
stem: If \(E\) and \(G\) respectively denote energy and gravitational constant, then \(\dfrac{E}{G}\) has the dimensions of
solution:
Dimensional formula of energy
\([E] = [M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]\) ...(I)
Dimensional formula of gravitational constant
\([G] = [M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}]\) ...(II)
From (I) & (II)
\(\dfrac{[E]}{[G]} = \dfrac{[M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]}{[M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}]} = [M^2 L^{-1} T^0]\)
Hence, dimensions of \(\left[\dfrac{E}{G}\right] = [M^2 L^{-1} T^0]\)
So, correct option is (1)

stem:
Match Column - I and Column - II and choose the correct match from the given choices.

| Column - I | Column - II |
|---|---|
| (A) Root mean square speed of gas molecules | (P) \(\dfrac{1}{3}nm\bar{v}^2\) |
| (B) Pressure exerted by ideal gas | (Q) \(\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}\) |
| (C) Average kinetic energy of a molecule | (R) \(\dfrac{5}{2}RT\) |
| (D) Total internal energy of 1 mole of a diatomic gas | (S) \(\dfrac{3}{2}k_B T\) |
solution:
Root mean square speed of gas molecule \(= \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}\)
Pressure exerted by ideal gas \(= \dfrac{1}{3}nm\bar{v}^2\)
Average kinetic energy of a molecule \(= \dfrac{3}{2}k_B T\)
Total internal energy of a gas is \((U) = \dfrac{1}{2}nfRT\)
Here, \(n = 1\), \(f = 5\)
\(U = \dfrac{5}{2}RT\)
Hence, (A) - (Q), (B) - (P), (C) - (S), (D) - (R)

subject: Physics
subtopic: Frequency of Potential Energy in SHM
stem: A body is executing simple harmonic motion with frequency \(n\), the frequency of its potential energy is
solution:
Equation of displacement of particle executing SHM is given by \(x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)\) ...(I)
Potential energy of particle executing SHM is given by
\(U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}kA^2\sin^2(\omega t + \phi)\) ...(II)
From I and II, it is clear that
Time period of \(x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)\) is
\(T_1 = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\) \(\Rightarrow\) frequency \(n_1 = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}\)
while time period of \(x^2 = A^2\sin^2(\omega t + \phi)\) is
\(T_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{\omega}\) \(\Rightarrow\) frequency \(n_2 = \dfrac{\omega}{\pi}\)
Hence \(n_2 = 2n_1\)

subject: Physics
stem: A cup of coffee cools from 90°C to 80°C in \(t\) minutes, when the room temperature is 20°C. The time taken by a similar cup of coffee to cool from 80°C to 60°C at a room temperature same at 20°C is
solution:
From Average form of Newton's law of cooling
\(-\left(\dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_s\right)K = \dfrac{T_1 - T_2}{\Delta t}\)
\(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are initial and final temperature and \(T_s\) is surrounding temperature.
\(\Rightarrow -K\left[\dfrac{(90 + 80)}{2} - 20\right] = \dfrac{90 - 80}{t}\)
\(\Rightarrow -K(65) = \dfrac{10}{t}\)
\(\Rightarrow K = \dfrac{-2}{13t}\)
In second case,
\(-K\left(\dfrac{80 + 60}{2} - 20\right) = \dfrac{(80 - 60)}{t_1}\)
\(\Rightarrow -K(50) = \dfrac{20}{t_1}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{2}{13t}(50) = \dfrac{20}{t_1}\)
\(\Rightarrow t_1 = \dfrac{13t}{5}\)

subject: Physics
stem: A capacitor of capacitance \(C\), is connected across an ac source of voltage \(V\), given by \(V = V_0\sin\omega t\). The displacement current between the plates of the capacitor, would then be given by
solution:
Given \(V = V_0\sin\omega t\) ...(1)
Now displacement current \(I_d\) is given by
\(I_d = C\dfrac{dV}{dt}\)
\(= C\dfrac{d}{dt}(V_0\sin\omega t)\) (using equation 1)
\(= C(V_0\omega)\cos\omega t\)
\(I_d = V_0\omega C\cos\omega t\)

subject: Physics
stem: The half-life of a radioactive nuclide is 100 hours. The fraction of original activity that will remain after 150 hours would be
solution:
The activity of a radioactive substance is given as
\(A = A_0\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}\)
Now, \(\dfrac{A}{A_0} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{A}{A_0} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{150/100}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{A}{A_0} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3/2}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{A}{A_0} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\)

subject: Physics
stem: An inductor of inductance \(L\), a capacitor of capacitance \(C\) and a resistor of resistance \(R\) are connected in series to an ac source of potential difference \(V\) volts as shown in figure. Potential difference across \(L\), \(C\) and \(R\) is 40 V, 10 V and 40 V, respectively. The amplitude of current flowing through \(LCR\) series circuit is \(10\sqrt{2}\) A. The impedance of the circuit is
solution:
\(V_L = 40\) volt
\(V_R = 40\) volt
\(V_C = 10\) volt
Now, \(V_{RMS} = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}\)
\(= \sqrt{(40)^2 + (40 - 10)^2} = 50\) V
\(I_{RMS} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{10\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 10\) A
\(\because V_{RMS} = I_{RMS}\times Z\)
\(\therefore Z = \dfrac{V_{RMS}}{I_{RMS}} = \dfrac{50}{10} = 5\ \Omega\)

subject: Physics
stem: A thick current carrying cable of radius \(R\) carries current \(I\) uniformly distributed across its cross-section. The variation of magnetic field \(B(r)\) due to the cable with the distance \(r\) from the axis of the cable is represented by
options: Graph (1): B increasing as a concave-up curve with r (B \(\propto r^2\)-like)
Graph (2): B increasing linearly with r throughout
Graph (3): B rising linearly up to r = R then falling as 1/r (hyperbola)
Graph (4): B rising and saturating (concave-down) with r
solution:
From Ampere's circuital law
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R^2}\cdot r\) if \(r < R \Rightarrow B_{inside}\propto r\)
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\) if \(r \geq R \Rightarrow B_{outside}\propto\dfrac{1}{r}\)
Hence the correct plot of magnetic field \(B\) with distance \(r\) from axis of cable is a straight line up to \(r = R\) (inside) and a hyperbola beyond (outside).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: An electromagnetic wave of wavelength \(\lambda\) is incident on a photosensitive surface of negligible work function. If \(m\) mass is of photoelectron emitted from the surface has de-Broglie wavelength \(\lambda_d\), then
solution:
As per Einstein's photoelectric equation
\(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \phi_0 + k\)
\(\phi_0\): work function
\(k\) = maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons
As per question, \(\phi\rightarrow0\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = k = \dfrac{P^2}{2m} \Rightarrow P = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mhc}{\lambda}}\)
Now De-broglie wavelength,
\(\lambda_d = \dfrac{h}{P} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mhc/\lambda}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \sqrt{\lambda} = \lambda_d\sqrt{\dfrac{2mc}{h}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \lambda = \left(\dfrac{2mc}{h}\right)\lambda_d^2\)

subject: Physics
stem: The escape velocity from the Earth's surface is \(v\). The escape velocity from the surface of another planet having a radius, four times that of Earth and same mass density is
solution:
Escape velocity from the Earth's surface
\(v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G\rho\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3}{R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8G\rho\pi}{3}R^2}\)
\(v_e\propto R\) (For same density)
\(\dfrac{v}{v_1} = \dfrac{R}{4R}\)
\(v_1 = 4v\)

subject: Physics
stem: If force \([F]\), acceleration \([A]\) and time \([T]\) are chosen as the fundamental physical quantities. Find the dimensions of energy.
solution:
Energy, \(E\propto F^a A^b T^c\)
\([E] = [F^a][A^b][T^c]\)
\(\Rightarrow [ML^2 T^{-2}] = [MLT^{-2}]^a [LT^{-2}]^b [T]^c\)
\([ML^2 T^{-2}] = [M^a L^{a+b} T^{-2a-2b+c}]\)
Comparing dimensions on both sides.
\(\Rightarrow a = 1;\ a + b = 2\) and \(-2 = -2a - 2b + c\)
\(\Rightarrow b = 1\) \(\Rightarrow -2 = -2 - 2 + c\)
\(\Rightarrow c = 2\)
\([E] = [FAT^2]\)

subject: Physics
stem: Two conducting circular loops of radii \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are placed in the same plane with their centres coinciding. If \(R_1 >> R_2\), the mutual inductance \(M\) between them will be directly proportional to
solution:
Two concentric coils are of radius \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) as shown. Let current in outer loop be \(i\)
Magnetic field at centre \(= B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2R_1}\)
Magnetic flux through inner coil \(= B\times\pi R_2^2\)
\(\phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2R_1}\times\pi R_2^2\)
\(\phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2}\times\dfrac{\pi R_2^2}{R_1}\)
as per definition, \(\phi = Mi\)
\(\Rightarrow M = \left(\dfrac{\mu_0\pi}{2}\right)\dfrac{R_2^2}{R_1}\)
\(\therefore M\propto\dfrac{R_2^2}{R_1}\)

subject: Physics
stem: A point object is placed at a distance of 60 cm from a convex lens of focal length 30 cm. If a plane mirror were put perpendicular to the principal axis of the lens and at a distance of 40 cm from it, the final image would be formed at a distance of
options: 20 cm from the lens, it would be a real image
30 cm from the lens, it would be a real image
30 cm from the plane mirror, it would be a virtual image
20 cm from the plane mirror, it would be a virtual image
solution:
Using lens formula for first refraction from convex lens
\(\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
\(v_1 = ?\), \(u = -60\) cm, \(f = 30\) cm
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v_1} + \dfrac{1}{60} = \dfrac{1}{30} \Rightarrow v_1 = 60\) cm
\(I_1\) here is first image by lens
The plane mirror will produce an image at distance 20 cm to left of it.
For second refraction from convex lens,
\(u = -20\) cm, \(v = ?\), \(f = 30\) cm
\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{30}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{20} \Rightarrow v = -60\) cm
Thus the final image is virtual and at a distance, \(60 - 40 = 20\) cm from plane mirror.

subject: Physics
stem: Three resistors having resistances \(r_1\), \(r_2\) and \(r_3\) are connected as shown in the given circuit. The ratio \(\dfrac{i_3}{i_1}\) of currents in terms of resistances used in the circuit is
solution:
In parallel combination of resistances \(r_2\) and \(r_3\), potential difference will be equal across both resistance.
So, \(i_2 r_2 = i_3 r_3 \Rightarrow i_2 = \dfrac{i_3 r_3}{r_2}\) ...(1)
As per Kirchhoff's first law
\(\Rightarrow i_1 = i_2 + i_3\)
\(\Rightarrow i_1 = \left(\dfrac{r_3}{r_2} + 1\right)i_3\) (from equation 1)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{i_3}{i_1} = \dfrac{r_2}{r_2+r_3}\)

subject: Physics
stem: For the given circuit, the input digital signals are applied at the terminals \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). What would be the output at the terminal \(y\)? (The circuit is an AND gate on inputs A, B feeding an OR gate, and a NAND gate on inputs B, C feeding the same OR gate; the input waveforms for A, B, C over intervals \(t_1\)–\(t_6\) are given.)
options: Waveform (1): y stays at 0 V throughout
Waveform (2): y high (5 V) only during t1–t3, else 0 V
Waveform (3): y stays high at 5 V throughout
Waveform (4): y high except a low pulse in t1–t2 and t3–t4
solution:
Output of combination of logic gates is given as
\(y = A\cdot B + \overline{B\cdot C}\)

Input/Output truth table over the time durations:

| Time duration | A | B | C | AB | \(\overline{B\cdot C}\) | \(y = A\cdot B + \overline{B\cdot C}\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 - \(t_1\) | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| \(t_1\) - \(t_2\) | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| \(t_2\) - \(t_3\) | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| \(t_3\) - \(t_4\) | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| \(t_4\) - \(t_5\) | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| \(t_5\) - \(t_6\) | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| \(t_6\) - \(t_7\) | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |

So the output \(y\) is high (1) that is \(v_0 = 5\) V

subject: Physics
stem: A series LCR circuit containing 5.0 H inductor, 80 \(\mu\)F capacitor and 40 \(\Omega\) resistor is connected to 230 V variable frequency ac source. The angular frequencies of the source at which power transferred to the circuit is half the power at the resonant angular frequency are likely to be
solution:
The resonance frequency of LCR series circuit is given as \(\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5\times80\times10^{-6}}} = 50\) rad/s
Now half power frequencies are given as
\(\omega = \omega_0 \pm \dfrac{R}{2L}\)
i.e. \(\omega_L = 50 - \dfrac{40}{2\times5} = 46\) rad/s
\(\omega_H = 50 + \dfrac{40}{2\times5} = 54\) rad/s

subject: Physics
stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 5 m/s\(^2\). At \(t = 4\) s, a ball is dropped out of a window by a person sitting in the car. What is the velocity and acceleration of the ball at \(t = 6\) s? (Take \(g = 10\) m/s\(^2\))
solution:
Initial velocity of car = 0
Acceleration of car = 5 m/s\(^2\)
Velocity of car at \(t = 4\) s; \(v = u + at\)
\(\Rightarrow v = 0 + 5\times4 = 20\) ms\(^{-1}\)
At \(t = 4\) s, A ball is dropped out of a window so velocity of ball at this instant is 20 ms\(^{-1}\) along horizontal.
After 2 seconds of motion :
Horizontal velocity of ball = 20 ms\(^{-1}\) \((\because a_x = 0)\)
Vertical velocity of ball \((v_y) = u_y + a_y t\)
\(v_y = 0 + 10\times2 = 20\) ms\(^{-1}\) \((\because a_y = g = 10\) m/s\(^2)\)
So magnitude of velocity of ball
\((v) = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = 20\sqrt{2}\) m/s
Acceleration of ball at \(t = 6\) s is \(g = 10\) m/s\(^2\)
As ball is under free fall.

subject: Physics
stem: A particle of mass \(m\) is projected with a velocity \(v = kV_e\) \((k < 1)\) from the surface of the earth. \((V_e = \text{escape velocity})\) The maximum height above the surface reached by the particle is
solution:
given \(v = kV_e\)
where, \(k < 1\)
Thus, \(v < V_e\)
From conservation of mechanical energy,
\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GmM}{R} = -\dfrac{GmM}{(R+h)}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{v^2}{2} = \dfrac{GM}{R} - \dfrac{(GM)}{(R+h)} = \dfrac{h}{R(R+h)}GM\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2}k^2 V_e^2 = \dfrac{GMh}{R(R+h)}\)
We know, \(V_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2}k^2\left(\dfrac{2GM}{R}\right) = \dfrac{GMh}{R(R+h)}\)
\(k^2 = \dfrac{h}{(R+h)}\)
\(Rk^2 + hk^2 = h\)
\(Rk^2 = h(1 - k^2)\)
\(\therefore h = \dfrac{Rk^2}{(1-k^2)}\)

subject: Physics
stem: A particle moving in a circle of radius \(R\) with a uniform speed takes a time \(T\) to complete one revolution. If this particle were projected with the same speed at an angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, the maximum height attained by it equals \(4R\). The angle of projection, \(\theta\), is then given by :
solution:
To complete a circular path of radius \(R\), time period is \(T\).
so speed of particle \((U) = \dfrac{2\pi R}{T}\) ......(1)
Now the particle is projected with same speed at angle \(\theta\) to horizontal.
So Maximum Height \((H) = \dfrac{U^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\)
Given that : \(H = 4R\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{U^2\sin^2\theta}{2g} = 4R\)
\(\Rightarrow \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{8gR}{U^2}\) ...(2)
\(\Rightarrow \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{8gRT^2}{4\pi^2 R^2} = \dfrac{2gT^2}{\pi^2 R}\) (using equation 1)
\(\Rightarrow \theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2gT^2}{\pi^2 R}\right)^{1/2}\)

subject: Physics
subtopic: Vector Cross Product in Magnetic Force
stem: In the product \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = q\vec{v}\times(B\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + B_0\hat{k})\). For \(q = 1\) and \(\vec{v} = 2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{F} = 4\hat{i} - 20\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}\). What will be the complete expression for \(\vec{B}\)?
solution:
\(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = q\vec{v}\times(B\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + B_0\hat{k})\)
Given, \(q = 1\), \(\vec{v} = 2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{F} = 4\hat{i} - 20\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}\)
\(\Rightarrow (4\hat{i} - 20\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}) = -1\times[(2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k})\times(B\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + B_0\hat{k})]\)
Thus, calculating values of RHS,
\(\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ 2 & 4 & 6\\ B & B & B_0\end{vmatrix}\)
\(\Rightarrow \hat{i}(4B_0 - 6B) - \hat{j}(2B_0 - 6B) + \hat{k}(2B - 4B)\)
Comparing L.H.S and R.H.S,
\(4B_0 - 6B = 4 \Rightarrow 2B_0 - 3B = 2\) ...(1)
\(-(2B_0 - 6B) = -20 \Rightarrow B_0 - 3B = 10\) ...(2)
\(2B - 4B = 12 \Rightarrow B = -6\) ...(3)
From (2) and (3)
\(B = -6\) and \(B_0 = -8\)
Hence, \(\vec{B} = -6\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}\)

subject: Physics
stem: A ball of mass 0.15 kg is dropped from a height 10 m, strikes the ground and rebounds to the same height. The magnitude of impulse imparted to the ball is \((g = 10\) m/s\(^2)\) nearly
solution:
Given that :
Mass of ball = 0.15 kg
Height from which ball is dropped = 10 m
Impulse, \(\vec{I}\) = Change in linear momentum = \(\Delta\vec{P}\)
\(= \vec{P_f} - \vec{P_i}\)
Velocity of ball at ground \((v) = \sqrt{2gh}\)
\(= \sqrt{2\times10\times10} = 10\sqrt{2}\) m/s
\(\vec{I} = 0.15\times10\sqrt{2}(-\hat{j}) - 0.15\times10\sqrt{2}(\hat{j})\)
\(\vec{I} = 2\times0.15\times10\sqrt{2}(-\hat{j}) = 4.2(-\hat{j})\)
\(\Rightarrow\) magnitude of impulse = 4.2 kg m/s

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetic Dipole Moment of Coil Shapes
stem:
A uniform conducting wire of length \(12a\) and resistance \(R\) is wound up as a current carrying coil in the shape of,
(i) an equilateral triangle of side \(a\).
(ii) a square of side \(a\).
The magnetic dipole moments of the coil in each case respectively are
solution:
Current in the loop will be \(\dfrac{V}{R} = I\) which is same for both loops.
Now magnetic moment of Triangle loop = \(NIA\)
\(M_1 = \left(\dfrac{12a}{3a}\right)\cdot I\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2 = \sqrt{3}Ia^2\)
and magnetic moment of square loop = \(N'IA'\)
\(= \left(\dfrac{12a}{4a}\right)\cdot I\cdot a^2\)
\(M_2 = 3Ia^2\)

subject: Physics
stem: Twenty seven drops of same size are charged at 200 V each. They combine to form a bigger drop. Calculate the potential of the bigger drop.
solution:
Electric potential due to a charged sphere \(= \dfrac{kQ}{R}\)
\(k = 9\times10^9\) N-m\(^2\)/C\(^2\)
\(Q\): charge on sphere
\(R\): Radius of sphere
Let charge and radius of smaller drop is \(q\) and \(r\) respectively
For smaller drop, \(V = \dfrac{kq}{r} = 220\) V
Let \(R\) be radius of bigger drop,
As volume remains the same
\(\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right)\times27 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3\)
\(\Rightarrow R = \sqrt[3]{27}\ r = 3r\)
Now, using charge conservation,
\(\Rightarrow Q = 27q\)
\(V_{big\ drop} = \dfrac{kQ}{R} = \dfrac{k(27q)}{3r} = 9\left(\dfrac{kq}{r}\right)\)
\(= 9\times220 = 1980\) V

subject: Physics
chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
stem: A uniform rod of length 200 cm and mass 500 g is balanced on a wedge placed at 40 cm mark. A mass of 2 kg is suspended from the rod at 20 cm and another unknown mass \(m\) is suspended from the rod at 160 cm mark as shown in the figure. Find the value of \(m\) such that the rod is in equilibrium. \((g = 10\) m/s\(^2)\)
solution:
Given that
Mass of rod = 500 g; Length of rod = 200 cm
Rod will be in equilibrium, when net torque about point \(O\) will be zero.
Torque at point \(O\) due to 2 kg mass
\(\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F} = rF\sin\theta(\hat{n})\)
\(\tau_1 = 20\times20\times10^{-2}\times\sin90°(\hat{k}) = 4\) N m\((\hat{k})\)
Torque due to mass of rod : (centre of mass at 100 cm, 60 cm from O)
\(\tau_2 = 5\times60\times10^{-2}\times\sin90°(-\hat{k}) = 3\) N m\((-\hat{k})\)
Torque due to mass \(m\)
\(\tau_3 = mg\times120\times10^{-2}\times\sin90°(-\hat{k}) = 12m\) N m\((-\hat{k})\)
Net torque about point \(O\) will be zero
So \(\vec{\tau_1} + \vec{\tau_2} + \vec{\tau_3} = 0\)
\(\Rightarrow 4 - 3 - 12m = 0\)
\(\Rightarrow 12m = 1\)
\(m = \dfrac{1}{12}\) kg

chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
subtopic: Moment of Inertia of Ring Segment
stem: From a circular ring of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) an arc corresponding to a 90° sector is removed. The moment of inertia of the remaining part of the ring about an axis passing through the centre of the ring and perpendicular to the plane of the ring is \(K\) times \(MR^2\). Then the value of \(K\) is
solution:
Given that,
Mass of Ring = \(M\); Radius of Ring = \(R\)
Now 90° arc is removed from circular ring, then mass removed = \(\dfrac{M}{4}\)
Mass of remaining portion = \(\dfrac{3M}{4}\)
Moment of inertia of remaining part = \(\int dmr^2\)
\(\Rightarrow I = R^2\int dm\) \((\because r = R)\)
\(\Rightarrow I = \dfrac{3MR^2}{4}\). So the value of \(K\) is \(\dfrac{3}{4}\)

subject: Physics
stem: A step down transformer connected to an ac mains supply of 220 V is made to operate at 11 V, 44 W lamp. Ignoring power losses in the transformer, what is the current in the primary circuit?
solution:
In ideal transformer:
Input power = Output power
\(\Rightarrow V_P I_P = V_S I_S = \text{Given power}\)
\(\Rightarrow 220\times I_P = 44\)
\(\Rightarrow I_P = 0.2\) A
